This article is noticing the bust and shockwave socialist countries went through post-socialism, and then goes on blaming capitalism as the root cause. There are several other factors:

  1. The people of Hungary (and other socialist nations) were economically kept behind for decades and hadn't the opportunity to invest into business or their skills as Western people had. When you break down the trade barriers and have Westerners suddenly freely acting on the free market, Westerners will obviously outperform natives in any open bidding. - This bust was inevitable however, as the Eastern economies were no longer viable and sooner or later had to open their borders for trade with the West to survive economically.

  2. Likewise, the existing native businesses were inefficient with too outdated machinery and too intensive labour use thanks to socialist "everyone works to provide for everyone" policy. That would inevitably lead to businesses either being outperformed by western competitors or sizing down and investing in increased productivity to become competitive. Either sends a lot of people to the streets without a job on the long term. - Again, this bust would have had to come sooner or later.

  3. The landgrab in early post-socialism wasn't very capitalistic, but heavily driven by nepotism, cronyism and cleptocracy. Socialist bureaucrats would sell choice plots for marvelous low prices to those who were connected to them and/or would bribe them personally, especially as they had no stake in actually making a profit on the sale as they wouldn't take part in it. I've seen it happen a lot of times with East Germany (such as the infamous bog of Sylt that was used to justify selling plots for vacation homes at 2DM/m² - only that no one but the responsible apparatchiks have ever witnessed it after 1990). And that was in East Germany where the West German Treuhandanstalt had at least some mitigating influence on the nepotistic hustling. In Hungary and other socialist countries not embedded into a Western law system, it was even worse.

You can't make an omelette without breaking some eggs, and when an economy had been dragged down by socialism for decades a lot of eggs will have to be broken in the recovery process. But recovery happens - Poland is a prime example, attracting a lot of business and industry and training its young people to skilled tradesmen earning vastly better wages in the west. - Or if you want a more long term example, look at Japan. The forced opening of their markets in 1869 vastly improved their knowledge, science and productivity to the point that they could dominate the Pacific Theatre in the 1930s. And in 1945, the forced conversion of their corporatist economy into a capitalist economy has led them from barely above subsistence income p.c. to one of the richest countries in the world.

A big factor is cargo capacity - there has never been a decent heavy lift Zeppelin. This limits their practical application as an economically viable transport. Yet, if one could be developed, it would open vast areas of new territory on the planet to economic expansion, areas such as Northern Canada, where building roads and rail networks remain prohibitively expensive. These areas are currently served almost exclusively by small aircraft, which limits what can be brought in in terms of heavy equipment, vehicles, and supplies.

Yes you can build a road or a railway, but there has to be a huge economic prize at the other end of that route to pay for it all. It costs more than ten times as much to build in the North as it does in the South. Transport is a huge factor. In American history, the interior could only be reached by wagon train until the arrival of the railways. Under such conditions major cities were simply not possible, so major cities grew only where water transport allowed bulk cargo access by ship.

One of my ancestors made his fortune organizing and operating huge wagon trains from Manitoba to the Klondike gold rush in the Yukon, delivering supplies for payment in pure gold.

http://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/klondike-gold-rush/

Supplying 100,000 people that far North was an extremely lucrative opportunity at the time.

From this perspective a heavy lift Zeppelin should be the ideal workhorse transport. Even the cost of fleet operations should be greatly discounted as compared to first building, and then operating a railway. The distances are vast, and current populations minimal.

How much lift capacity? A 100 car cargo train can haul upwards to 200+ transport trucks worth of cargo in a single train. A train can drive an entire loaded boxcar at a price of $1 per mile. Figure a Zeppelin would have to lift at least a couple of standard shipping containers, if not 10 of them. So the airship would need to be sizable indeed, and you would require a whole fleet of such ships.

There is probably also opportunity for something like this in major metro areas, where the population density has already maxed out almost all existing transportation options. The ability to move supplies into these areas remains a key limiting factor to even greater population density.
